title: Just watched Force Majeure with my brother and we had completely different interpretations so now I'm curious what others took from it

commenti.body:
I lean more towards your take also. Tomas, given his refusal for so long to admit to what he did, is of course not 100% in the right and therefore one can sympathise with Ebba.

However, Ebba's constantly made argument that she'd never behave the way he did and the implication that he's failed to live up to the standard of how a man or a parent should behave is later undermined at the end of the film. In the bus scene, Ebba also ends up abandoning the kids, which I guess is Östlund suggesting that nobody really knows how they'd react in a crisis.

Also, given that Tomas nor any of the other characters chastise Ebba for having abandoned her kids, I feel as though Östlund is saying that we shouldn't be too hard on ourselves or others for failing to live up to an ideal (as a man, as a mother, etc) even though one should still make the effort to do so.

This might be a wild interpretation on my part, but I think the scene near the end where Ebba gets herself in trouble and Tomas has to go save her was deliberately staged by Ebba herself in order to re-assert (or possibly further test) Tomas as living up to the ideal of a man/husband. Note how we don't really see much of what happens in this scene. I think there are various reasons why Ebba would have done this, but one of them would be that (at least for the kids' sake) she needs Tomas to regain his masculine/fatherly identity rather than continue to exist in the pitiable state he gets reduced to when he finally admits to having not behaved as he ideally should have.

At the time I watched the film I didn't really notice what you mentioned about the scene with the photographs, though I'm not saying your interpretation of that is wrong.

I do think you're right about the scene where she talks with the other woman about relationships. Ebba is definitely angry at her, but I think her anger stems precisely from Ebba's perception that the other woman isn't trying to live up to the ideal (from Ebba's perspective) of how a woman or wife should be. I think she's also angry in that scene, as you say, because of her marital issues with Tomas and so being presented with the alternative lifestyle the other woman follows forces her to confront the limitations or challenges posed by her own lifestyle/ideal of marriage.

Though it's not stated as explicitly as it could be, I think the film suggests pretty clearly that the reason the family are even on their ski holiday is because of issues in Ebba and Tomas' married life prior to what we see, like the 'workaholic' stuff you rightly point out.

Great film, and I definitely agree that Östlund deliberately leaves room for different interpretations.

The whole event sets Thomas up to eventually find a real deep look into his inner self. He denies it initially, but in the hotel scene he totally breaks down saying he is pathetic, how he cheats on board games with his kids. After that he is really changed just by that realization.

For Ebba we don't get this chance because the movie ends after her incident, but who knows she might eventually see that she had the same reaction.

I also really like the meta of Thormund Giantsbane guy and his girlfriend as the outside critics on this event, who are arguing between them like the audience essentially.

One of the best movies I've seen this year.

Btw if you liked this one, you'll love Anatomy of a Fall!

I agree with your view, not your brother's view. The film is certainly criticising Tomas and sympathetic to Ebba, but it's not trying to suggest that there's some kind of ideal standard of masculinity which Tomas is failing to live up to. The issue is the standard *itself*, which Tomas believes in so deeply he's can't even seem to be honest with himself when he fails to meet it, let alone his family. This is what makes the film brilliant!

The open relationship scene: your instinct on this scene is much more perceptive than your brother's. Ebba's rather conservative reaction is really just frustration at the idea that there are models of relationships beyond the unhappy and restrictive one she finds herself in.

The climactic scene on the slope is bittersweet because clearly an exhausted Ebba realises it's easier to sustain Tomas's pathetic ideas about 'being a man' and lie to preserve his self-image than it is to work out the more fundamental crack in their relationship.

Masculinity is bullshit: that's the film's message.

I really really don’t think it’s saying masculinity is bullshit. I think a lot of Ostlunds films challenge masculinity in the modern civilised society. He mocks it a lot but I think it’s far more nuanced than you are giving it credit for. With a lot more empathy towards men than just mockery.

I said 'masculinity is bullshit', not 'men are bullshit'. A character like Tomas is stunted by his narrow conception of what it means to be a man; his sense of 'masculinity' is just completely incompatible with the modern world he inhabits.  

I don't think the film criticises him for running for his life at the impending avalanche, for example. We get the sense that Ebba, the children and also the viewer would fully understand if he came back to the table, apologised for his selfish action in the heat of the moment and admitted his fear. 

The thing the film criticises him for is lying after the event. The idea of masculinity has tangled up his sense of self-worth with his image of himself 'as a man', and this prevents him from being able to admit the truth (he was afraid) and apologise. The fact he's more willing to damage his marriage by lying than admit to himself that he didn't live up to his own standard of masculinity shows that it's the standard he believes in that's the true issue here.

So yes, as well as mocking him, I think the film also empathetically observes just how pathetic men are. Masculinity represents the 'mind forg'd manacles' modern men are constrained by.
Just came here to say I had the exact same wild interpretation. I feel validated.
